issues.legal_issue: An appeal under the civil procedure code is not maintainable when it is directed only against a finding and not against a decree or an appealable order.
material_facts: The defendants’ appeal as originally filed challenged only the finding that the partition was a sham and sought a declaration that it was genuine.
The appeal did not challenge any part of the preliminary decree.
issues.conclusion: The appeal, as originally filed, was not maintainable because it was directed against a mere finding.
issues.legal_principle: The right of appeal is conferred by statute, unlike the general right to bring a civil suit. Under sections 96, 100, 104(1) and 105(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lies from a decree or from an order for which an appeal is expressly provided; Order 43, Rule 1 specifies appealable orders. The Code provides no appeal against a mere finding.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party brings an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.appeal_targets_only_a_finding: The appeal challenges a finding but does not challenge a decree or an appealable order.

issues.definition: When a party brings an appeal that challenges only a finding, the appeal is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Allowing an amendment that introduces a challenge to a decree after a long, unexplained delay, without seeking condonation and when rights have accrued to the decree-holder, is an improper exercise of judicial discretion.
material_facts: The defendants applied to amend their appeal more than seven years after filing it, seeking for the first time to challenge the preliminary decree.
They gave no explanation for the delay and did not apply for its condonation.
The preliminary decree had remained unchallenged, and the decree-holder had purchased the property at an auction sale in satisfaction of the decree.
The defendants had not used available opportunities to pay the decretal amount or seek to set aside the sale.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have allowed the amendment; doing so was not a proper exercise of judicial discretion.
issues.legal_principle: The power to allow amendments is wide and may be exercised at any stage in the interests of justice, notwithstanding limitation, but it is governed by judicial considerations. The wider the discretion, the greater the required care and circumspection. Allowing a belated amendment without good cause is improper where a valuable right has accrued to the opposing party.

rule.if: appeal_amendment_proceeding and amendment_introduces_challenge_to_decree and long_delay_unexplained and condonation_not_sought and decree_holder_rights_accrued

predicates.appeal_amendment_proceeding: A party seeks to amend a memorandum of appeal during an appeal proceeding.
predicates.amendment_introduces_challenge_to_decree: The proposed amendment adds a challenge to a decree that the original appeal did not contest.
predicates.long_delay_unexplained: The amendment is sought after a long delay for which the applicant provides no explanation.
predicates.condonation_not_sought: The applicant does not seek condonation of the delay.
predicates.decree_holder_rights_accrued: A valuable right has accrued to the decree-holder while the decree remained unchallenged.

issues.definition: If an amendment in an appeal adds a challenge to a decree after a long unexplained delay, condonation is not sought, and rights have accrued to the decree-holder, the amendment should not be allowed.

issues.legal_issue: A finding on an issue that was unnecessary to the decision and was not directly and substantially in issue does not operate as res judicata so as to support an appeal against that finding alone.
material_facts: The trial court’s decree restricted recovery to the father’s interest because the mortgage debt was not binding on the sons’ interests.
Whether the later partition was genuine did not affect that decree; even a genuine partition would not have made the mortgage binding on the sons’ interests.
The finding about the partition was unnecessary to the decision and the partition issue was not directly and substantially in issue in the suit.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the partition was a sham could not operate as res judicata, and the appeal against that finding was not maintainable on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the submission relying on Harchandra Das v. Bholanath Day, where the possibility of an appeal against a finding was linked to whether it would operate as res judicata. It did not decide whether that general view was correct; it held that the finding in this case was unnecessary to the decree and that the partition matter was not directly and substantially in issue, so the finding could not operate as res judicata.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and appeal_targets_only_a_finding and finding_unnecessary_to_decree and issue_not_directly_and_substantially_in_issue

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party brings an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.appeal_targets_only_a_finding: The appeal challenges a finding but does not challenge a decree or an appealable order.
predicates.finding_unnecessary_to_decree: The finding does not affect the decree because the same decree would follow even if the finding were resolved differently.
predicates.issue_not_directly_and_substantially_in_: The issue addressed by the finding was not directly and substantially in issue in the proceeding.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges only a finding that was unnecessary to the decree and concerned an issue not directly and substantially in issue, that finding does not operate as res judicata.
